about: Worked examples for prompts/extract-rules.md. All passages come from parts of the Ontario MTO handbook outside the passing topic, so none of them is scored. Each example has its own topic; the statements cover everything in the passages that is in scope for that topic, and nothing else.

examples.title: A definition and a fact in one passage
examples.teaches: Split a passage into one statement per proposition. 'Can' that describes what something does is not a permission, so it gives a FACT, not a MAY rule.

passages.page: Driving at night and in bad weather
passages.text: Fog is a thin layer of cloud resting on the ground. Fog can reduce visibility for drivers, resulting in difficult driving conditions.

statements.text: DEFINE fog IS a thin layer of cloud THAT rests on the ground

sources.quote: Fog is a thin layer of cloud resting on the ground.

statements.text: FACT fog can reduce visibility for drivers, resulting in difficult driving conditions

sources.quote: Fog can reduce visibility for drivers, resulting in difficult driving conditions.

statements.note: "Can" describes what fog does, not something a driver is allowed to do, so this is a FACT and not a MAY rule.

examples.title: A condition held in the heading and a list lead
examples.teaches: The list item never mentions fog. The heading and the lead sentence do, so the condition goes into the statement and both passages are cited. The lead sentence also holds rules of its own.

passages.page: Driving at night and in bad weather
passages.sec: Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog · ¶1
passages.text: Before you drive - and during your trip - check weather forecasts. If there is a fog warning, delay your trip until it clears. If you are caught driving in fog, follow these safe-driving tips:

passages.page: Driving at night and in bad weather
passages.sec: Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 3
passages.text: Use your low-beam headlights. High beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog, making it harder to see.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD check weather forecasts WHEN the driver is about to drive OR the driver is on a trip

sources.quote: Before you drive - and during your trip - check weather forecasts.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD delay the trip WHEN there is a fog warning UNTIL the fog clears

sources.quote: If there is a fog warning, delay your trip until it clears.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD use low-beam headlights WHEN driving in fog BECAUSE high beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog, making it harder to see

sources.quote: If you are caught driving in fog, follow these safe-driving tips:
Use your low-beam headlights. High beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog, making it harder to see.

statements.note: The item does not mention fog; the condition comes from the heading and the lead sentence, so it is written as WHEN driving in fog.

examples.title: Legal force from the section, and a sign caption
examples.topic: regulatory signs that tell drivers where they may not go or stop
examples.teaches: A sign caption is a bare imperative, which gives SHOULD by default. The section introduction says these signs must be obeyed, so the force is legal, and force_from names the section. The sentence about sign shapes is out of this topic and gives nothing.

passages.text: These signs give a direction that must be obeyed. They are usually rectangular or square with a white or black background and black, white or coloured letters. A sign with a green circle means you may or must do the activity shown inside the ring. A red circle with a line through it means the activity shown is not allowed.

passages.sec: Regulatory signs › Here are some common regulatory signs: · ¶4
Regulatory signs › Here are some common regulatory signs: · image
Regulatory signs › Here are some common regulatory signs: · ¶5
passages.text: Do not stop in the area between the signs. This means you may not stop your vehicle in this area, even for a moment. (Used in pairs or groups.)

statements.text: FACT a red circle with a line through it on a regulatory sign means the activity shown is not allowed

sources.quote: A red circle with a line through it means the activity shown is not allowed.

statements.force_from: context (Regulatory signs: "These signs give a direction that must be obeyed")
statements.text: a driver MUST NOT enter a road WHEN a "do not enter" sign is posted for the road

sources.quote: These signs give a direction that must be obeyed.
Do not enter this road.
a regulatory sign

statements.note: The caption alone is a bare imperative; the legal force comes from the section introduction.

statements.text: a driver MUST NOT stop the vehicle, even for a moment, WHEN the vehicle is in the area between "do not stop" signs

sources.quote: These signs give a direction that must be obeyed.
Do not stop in the area between the signs. This means you may not stop your vehicle in this area, even for a moment.

examples.title: Imperatives, a legal marker in the next sentence, UNTIL, and vague words
examples.teaches: "Never" alone gives SHOULD NOT; "It is illegal" in the next sentence makes it MUST NOT. A fixed distance in a bare imperative stays SHOULD with an M flag. "Until you are sure" is UNTIL with a J flag. Numbers become digits with the handbook's unit.

passages.text: When you come to a railway crossing, remember:
If a train is coming, stop at least five metres from the nearest rail or gate. Do not cross the track until you are sure the train or trains have passed.
Never drive around, under or through a railway gate or barrier while it is down, being lowered or being raised. It is illegal and dangerous.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD stop at least 5 m from the nearest rail or gate WHEN the driver comes to a railway crossing AND a train is coming

sources.quote: When you come to a railway crossing, remember:
If a train is coming, stop at least five metres from the nearest rail or gate.

flags.note: A fixed distance reads like a legal duty, but the sentence has no legal wording, so it stays SHOULD.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD NOT cross the track WHEN the driver comes to a railway crossing AND a train is coming UNTIL the driver is [?sure] the train or trains have passed

sources.quote: When you come to a railway crossing, remember:
Do not cross the track until you are sure the train or trains have passed.

statements.text: a driver MUST NOT drive around, under or through a railway gate or barrier WHILE the gate or barrier is down, being lowered or being raised BECAUSE it is dangerous

sources.quote: Never drive around, under or through a railway gate or barrier while it is down, being lowered or being raised. It is illegal and dangerous.

statements.note: "Never" alone would give SHOULD NOT; the next sentence, "It is illegal", gives legal force.

examples.title: An exception in the same passage is UNLESS
examples.teaches: "This does not apply if …" sits in the same passage as its rule, so it becomes an UNLESS clause. Clauses follow the fixed order WHEN, WHILE, ONLY IF, UNLESS, UNTIL, BECAUSE, IF VIOLATED.

passages.text: When you approach an intersection on a main road, and the intersection is blocked with traffic, stop before entering the intersection and wait until the traffic ahead moves on. This does not apply if you are turning left or right.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD stop before entering the intersection AND wait WHEN the driver approaches an intersection on a main road AND the intersection is blocked with traffic UNLESS the driver is turning left OR the driver is turning right UNTIL the traffic ahead moves on

sources.quote: When you approach an intersection on a main road, and the intersection is blocked with traffic, stop before entering the intersection and wait until the traffic ahead moves on. This does not apply if you are turning left or right.

statements.note: The exception is in the same passage, so it is an UNLESS clause. In a different passage it would be its own statement: EXCEPTION TO ex5a WHEN the driver is turning left OR the driver is turning right.

examples.title: A procedure, with a step that holds on its own
examples.teaches: Numbered steps make one PROCEDURE. The lead sentence gives its goal and condition. Each step cites its own passage. A conditional detour inside a step becomes an IF … THEN branch. A prohibition that holds whatever the step order is also written as its own RULE, linked to the procedure.

passages.text: When you need to stop by the side of the road for a short time to check something outside your vehicle, or to look for directions on a map, for example, follow these directions:
Before slowing down, check your mirrors and blind spot to see when the way is clear.

Turn on your signal before slowing down unless there are vehicles waiting to enter the road from side roads or driveways between you and the point where you intend to stop. Wait until you have passed these entrances so that drivers will not think you are turning before the stopping point.

Steer to the side of the road, steadily reducing speed, and stop parallel to the curb or edge of the road. You should not be more than about 30 centimetres away from it. Do not stop where you will block an entrance or other traffic.
Turn off your signal and turn on your hazard lights.

statements.text: TO make a roadside stop WHEN the driver needs to stop by the side of the road for a short time

steps.text: check the mirrors and blind spot to see when the way is clear WHEN the driver is about to slow down
turn on the signal WHEN the driver is about to slow down UNLESS vehicles are waiting to enter the road from side roads or driveways between the driver and the stopping point
steer to the side of the road, steadily reducing speed, AND stop parallel to the curb or edge of the road, at most [?about] 30 cm from it
turn off the signal AND turn on the hazard lights
IF vehicles are waiting to enter the road between the driver and the stopping point THEN turn on the signal only after passing these entrances

sources.quote: When you need to stop by the side of the road for a short time to check something outside your vehicle, or to look for directions on a map, for example, follow these directions:

flags.note: Approximate distance with no stated tolerance.

statements.note: The IF branch exists so that waiting drivers do not think the driver is turning before the stopping point.

statements.text: a driver SHOULD NOT stop where the vehicle will block an entrance or other traffic WHEN making a roadside stop

sources.quote: Do not stop where you will block an entrance or other traffic.

statements.note: This prohibition holds whatever the step order, so it is its own RULE as well as part of step 3's situation.

examples.title: A duty and its penalty in different passages, and choosing the role
examples.teaches: A duty and its penalty make one statement with IF VIOLATED, citing both passages. "You" can cover more than one role; use the role each sentence supports. A penalty with no separate duty sentence still makes a legal rule, with force from the penalty.

passages.text: You must use your seatbelt every time you travel in any vehicle equipped with seatbelts. All passengers must be buckled up in their own seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

Drivers who do not buckle up can be fined and will be given two demerit points. Drivers may also be fined and receive demerit points if they fail to ensure that all passengers under 16 years of age are properly buckled in a seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

statements.text: a driver MUST use a seatbelt WHILE travelling in a vehicle equipped with seatbelts IF VIOLATED a fine AND 2 demerit points

sources.quote: You must use your seatbelt every time you travel in any vehicle equipped with seatbelts.
Drivers who do not buckle up can be fined and will be given two demerit points.

statements.note: The duty and its penalty are in different paragraphs, so they make one statement. "You" also covers passengers, but the penalty names drivers; the passenger duty is ex7b.

statements.text: a passenger MUST be buckled up in the passenger's own seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat

sources.quote: All passengers must be buckled up in their own seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

statements.force_from: context (penalty: "may also be fined and receive demerit points")
statements.text: a driver MUST ensure that every passenger under 16 years of age is [?properly] buckled in a seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat IF VIOLATED a fine AND demerit points

sources.quote: Drivers may also be fined and receive demerit points if they fail to ensure that all passengers under 16 years of age are properly buckled in a seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

flags.note: The handbook does not say what proper buckling requires.

statements.note: Only the penalty is stated; a penalty for failing to do something makes doing it a legal duty. The number of demerit points is not given, so none is written.

examples.title: "Pass" that does not mean overtaking
examples.teaches: Here "pass" means that oncoming bicycles go by; nobody overtakes anyone. The sentence is a left-turn rule, which is outside the passing topic, so a passing extraction writes no statement for it. Writing nothing is the right answer for such passages.

passages.page: Sharing the road with other road users
passages.sec: Sharing the road with cyclists · item 6
passages.text: When turning left, you must stop and wait for oncoming bicycles to pass before turning.
